topics.title: Composite Functions
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: understand and use function notation. (k u s)
describe and understand a composite function. (k u s)
work out the inverse of a function and recognise the graphical relationship between a function and its inverse. (k u s)

body.text: A boda boda rider in Kampala works out a fare from the distance of a trip. On a rainy day, he then adds an extra charge. Each step is a rule that turns one number into another. In mathematics such a rule is called a function, and doing one rule after another gives a composite function.
A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. We write f(x), read as "f of x", for the output when the input is x. For example, f(x) = 6x means "multiply the input by 6".

body.speech: f of x equals 6x, so f of 3 equals 6 times 3, which is 18

body.text: The set of inputs is called the domain. The set of outputs is called the range. You met these ideas in Senior 2 mappings and relations.
A function does not have to be a formula. Suppose f(x) is the greatest prime number less than x. Then f(40) = 37 and f(29) = 23. Each input still gives exactly one output.

A composite function applies one function and then another. We write gf(x), or g(f(x)), to mean: first apply f to x, then apply g to the result. Always work from the inside out, so the function nearest to x acts first.

body.speech: g f of x equals g of f of x

body.title: The order matters
steps: So gf(3) and fg(3) are different. The order of the functions matters.

body.text: The notation f²(x) means f(f(x)), so f is applied twice. It does not mean f(x) squared. With f(x) = 6x, f²(5) = f(30) = 180, and in general f²(x) = 36x.

body.title: A rainy-day boda boda fare
steps: A rider charges f(d) = 1,000 + 500d shillings for a trip of d km. On rainy days he raises any fare F by 20%, using the rule g(F) = 1.2F.
The rainy-day fare applies f first, then g, so it is gf(d).
For a 6 km trip from the taxi park to Ntinda: gf(6) = 1,200 + 600 × 6 = 4,800.
Check in two steps: f(6) = 1,000 + 3,000 = 4,000, and g(4,000) = 1.2 × 4,000 = 4,800. The rainy-day fare is UGX 4,800.

body.text: The inverse of a function undoes it. If f sends 3 to 18, the inverse sends 18 back to 3. We write the inverse as f⁻¹(x). Here the −1 is a label. It does not mean 1 divided by f(x).

body.title: Inverse of a linear function
steps: Make y the subject: x − 3 = 2y, so y = (x − 3)/2.
Check: f(4) = 2 × 4 + 3 = 11, and f⁻¹(11) = (11 − 3)/2 = 4. The inverse brings us back to the start.

body.title: Inverse of a composite function
steps: Let f(x) = 2x³ and g(x) = x − 1. Find h(x) = f(g(x)) and its inverse.
Write y = 2(x − 1)³ and swap x and y: x = 2(y − 1)³.
Divide by 2: (y − 1)³ = x/2. Take the cube root: y − 1 = ∛(x/2).

body.text: The graph of a function and its inverse

Draw y = f(x) and y = f⁻¹(x) on the same axes, using the same scale on both. Also draw the line y = x. The graph of the inverse is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x. This happens because finding the inverse swaps x and y, so each point (a, b) becomes (b, a).

Some functions have no inverse over their whole domain. For f(x) = x², both 3 and −3 give 9, so 9 cannot be sent back to a single number. If we use only x ≥ 0 as the domain, the inverse is √x. The range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

body.title: Function machines
body.text: In pairs, write f(x) = 6x on one card and g(x) = x + 5 on another, as two function machines. One partner chooses a number and passes it through f and then g. The other passes the same number through g and then f. Compare the results for several numbers. Then, on squared paper with the same scale on both axes, plot f(x) = 2x + 3 and f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2 for x from −3 to 3. Draw the line y = x, fold the paper along it and see what happens to the two graphs.
Does every function have an inverse? Think about a rule that sends two different inputs to the same output, such as a boda boda fare rounded to the nearest 1,000 shillings.

f(x) is the output of f when the input is x. gf(x) means apply f first, then g, and usually fg(x) is not the same as gf(x). To find f⁻¹, swap x and y and make y the subject. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.
